title: Does breathing limit performance?
goal: Judge when the respiratory system limits endurance performance, through the cost of breathing, diaphragm fatigue and the metaboreflex, and what respiratory muscle training can and can't do.

steps.title: What breathing costs
steps.text:
Breathing 150 L·min⁻¹ is hard work for the [diaphragm](g:diaphragm) and the other breathing muscles. At maximal exercise the O₂ cost of breathing averaged about **10% of VO₂max**, and 13–15% in people who used most of their breathing reserve. The cost climbs steeply near the top: from heavy to maximal exercise, 39% of the extra O₂ went to breathing, against 8% at moderate intensity [[c:o2-cost]].

Blood follows the O₂. At maximal exercise, up to **14–16% of [cardiac output](g:cardiac-output)** goes to the breathing muscles [[c:co-share]].

So near the top of a hard climb or a 1,500 m race, the breathing muscles compete with the legs for O₂ and blood.

claims.text: At maximal exercise the O₂ cost of breathing averaged 10% of VO₂max (13–15% in those near their mechanical limits), and its share of each extra step in O₂ uptake rose from 8% at moderate intensity to 39% from heavy to maximal exercise.

evidence.quote: At maximum exercise, the O2 cost of ventilation (VE) averaged 10 +/- 0.7% of the VO2max.
In subjects who used most of their maximum reserve for expiratory flow and for inspiratory muscle pressure development during maximum exercise, the VO2RM required 13-15% of VO2max.

The O2 cost of increasing VE from one work rate to the next rose from 8% of the increase in total body VO2 (VO2T) during moderate exercise to 39 +/- 10% in the transition from heavy to maximum exercise

claims.text: At maximal exercise, up to 14–16% of cardiac output goes to the respiratory muscles.

evidence.quote: up to 14-16% of the CO is directed to the respiratory muscles

steps.title: How much O₂ goes to breathing?
steps.problem: A cyclist's VO₂max is 4.0 L·min⁻¹. Breathing costs about 10% of that at maximal effort. How much O₂ do his breathing muscles use, and how much is left for everything else?
steps: Left for the legs and the rest of the body: 4.0 − 0.4 = 3.6 L·min⁻¹.

steps.title: Can the diaphragm tire?
steps.text:
Yes, in hard enough exercise. In 12 healthy people, the diaphragm's force in response to nerve stimulation fell by 8–32% after exercise to exhaustion at 95% of VO₂max. It took about 70 min to recover almost fully, and fatigue became more likely and larger as intensity rose above 85% of VO₂max [[c:diaphragm-fatigue]].

This fits the cost card: the work of breathing climbs steeply near the top. A long ride or run well below that intensity asks much less of the diaphragm.

The measurement trick matters: stimulating the phrenic nerve (the nerve to the diaphragm) electrically, through the skin, tests the muscle itself, so a lower force can't be blamed on low motivation.

claims.text: After exercise to exhaustion at 95% VO₂max, stimulated diaphragm force fell 8–32%, recovering almost fully by about 70 min; fatigue grows as intensity exceeds 85% VO₂max.

evidence.quote: Following exercise at 95% of VO2, max, group mean Pdi twitch values were reduced at all lung volumes (range -8 +/- 3 to -32 +/- 5%)
Stimulated Pdi values recovered partially by 30 min post-exercise and almost completely by an average time of 70 min.
The magnitude of the fatigue and the likelihood of its occurrence increases as the relative intensity of the exercise exceeds 85% of VO2, max.

steps.title: The metaboreflex: breathing takes leg blood
steps.text:
When breathing muscles tire, their metabolites trigger a reflex, the [respiratory muscle metaboreflex](g:metaboreflex), that narrows blood vessels in the limbs. At rest, fatiguing breathing work cut leg blood flow by about 30% [[c:sheel-rest]].

At VO₂max, cyclists had their breathing work lowered by a ventilator or raised by a resistor. A ±50% change moved leg blood flow by about 2 L·min⁻¹ (11%) [[c:harms-flow]]. At 90% of VO₂max, unloading the breathing muscles lengthened time to exhaustion by 14%; loading shortened it by 15% [[c:harms-tte]].

The proposed chain: breathing work → breathing-muscle fatigue → reflex → less leg blood flow → earlier leg fatigue [[c:chain]].

claims.text: At rest, fatiguing diaphragm work reduced leg blood flow by about 30%, attributed to a metaboreflex from the diaphragm.

evidence.quote: subsequently decreased (-30 %) and LVR increased (50-60 %) relative to control in a time-dependent manner
We attribute these changes to a metaboreflex originating in the diaphragm.

claims.text: At VO₂max, a ±50% change in the work of breathing changed leg blood flow by about 2 L·min⁻¹ (11%): normal breathing work compromises leg perfusion.

evidence.quote: For a +/-50% change from control in Wb, Qlegs changed 2 l/min or 11% of control
We conclude that Wb normally incurred during maximal exercise causes vasoconstriction in locomotor muscles and compromises locomotor muscle perfusion and VO2.

claims.text: At 90% VO₂max, unloading the respiratory muscles increased time to exhaustion by 14% and loading reduced it by 15%, in seven trained male cyclists.

evidence.quote: Time to exhaustion was increased with unloading in 76% of the trials by an average of 1.3 +/- 0.4 min or 14 +/- 5% and decreased with loading in 83% of the trials by an average of 1.0 +/- 0.6 min or 15 +/- 3% compared with control

claims.text: Proposed chain: respiratory muscle fatigue triggers a metaboreflex that raises sympathetic vasoconstriction, cutting locomotor muscle blood flow and causing leg fatigue.

evidence.quote: A key step in this linkage is a respiratory muscle fatigue-induced metaboreflex, which increases sympathetic vasoconstrictor outflow, causing reduced blood flow to locomotor muscles and locomotor muscle fatigue.

debate.question: Does the respiratory system limit endurance performance in healthy athletes?

sides.position: Yes, in fit athletes at high intensity: breathing work steals leg blood flow, unloading it improves endurance, and ventilation can reach limiting levels.
Mostly not: the O₂ cost of breathing is large but not enough to cap useful ventilation, and in most people gas exchange keeps pace with metabolism.

steps.title: Does training the breathing muscles help?
steps.text:
[Respiratory muscle training](g:rmt) (RMT) means breathing against a resistance, or breathing hard for long spells, a few times a week.

- It reliably makes inspiratory muscles stronger: maximal inspiratory pressure (the hardest suck against a blocked mouthpiece) rose by about 29 cmH₂O in athletes, with no change in lung function [[c:rmt-strength]].
- Performance improves by a moderate amount: an [effect size](g:effect-size) of 0.64 for inspiratory training in athletes, seen in time trials and time-to-exhaustion tests [[c:rmt-performance]].
- Less fit people gain more, and standard ramp tests often miss the effect [[c:rmt-who]].

The trials are small and their protocols and outcomes differ [[c:rmt-limits]]. For a trained cyclist or runner: a modest gain is plausible, a big one is not.

claims.text: Inspiratory muscle training raises maximal inspiratory pressure (about 29 cmH₂O in athletes) without changing lung function.

evidence.quote: IMT-linear improved maximal inspiratory pressure (MD -29.42 cmH2O [-35.65, -23.20]; p < 0.001), independent of sports modality.
There was no influence of IMT on the maximal expiratory pressure and pulmonary function markers.
Inspiratory muscle strength and endurance improved in most studies, which in part, was dependent on the type of RMT employed.

claims.text: RMT improves sport performance by a moderate amount (SMD 0.64 for inspiratory training in athletes), shown in time trials and endurance-time tests.

evidence.quote: It was observed that IMT-linear improves the sports performance (SMD 0.64 [0.35, 0.92]; p < 0.0001) with moderate effect size.
Meta-analyses demonstrated a significant positive effect of RMT on sport performance outcomes of time trials, exercise endurance time, and repetitions on Yo-Yo tests.
RMT improves endurance exercise performance in healthy individuals with greater improvements in less fit individuals and in sports of longer durations.

claims.text: Less fit people benefit more from RMT (6% more per 10 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ lower VO₂max), and conventional incremental tests fail to detect the improvement.

evidence.quote: less fit subjects benefit more from RMT than highly trained athletes (6.0% per 10 mL · kg⁻¹ · min⁻¹ decrease in maximal oxygen uptake

The meta-analysis, performed on eight controlled trials revealed a significant improvement in performance after RMT, which was detected by constant load tests, time trials and intermittent incremental tests, but not by conventional incremental tests.

claims.text: The RMT evidence is limited by small samples, differing protocols and differing outcome measures.

evidence.quote: Determination of the type of athlete that may benefit most from RMT was limited by small sample sizes, differing RMT protocols, and differences in outcome measures across studies.

points: At maximal exercise breathing costs about 10% of VO₂max (up to 15%) and takes up to 14–16% of cardiac output; the cost rises steeply near the top.
Exercise to exhaustion above about 85% of VO₂max can fatigue the diaphragm.
Tiring breathing muscles trigger a metaboreflex that narrows leg vessels and cuts leg blood flow; unloading them extended endurance in small studies of trained men.
The lung is a limit mainly for fit athletes at high intensity (metaboreflex, EIAH); at moderate intensity it copes.
Respiratory muscle training reliably strengthens inspiratory muscles and modestly improves performance, more in less fit people; the trials are small and varied.

variants.stem: At VO₂max, how can hard breathing cut blood flow to the legs?

options.text: Tiring breathing muscles trigger a reflex that narrows leg blood vessels
options.why: Right: the respiratory muscle metaboreflex raises sympathetic vasoconstriction in the limbs.

options.text: The inflated lungs squeeze the heart, so it pumps less
options.why: Cardiac output wasn't lowered by heavier breathing work; it is the share going to the legs that falls.

options.text: The breathing muscles use up the blood's O₂ before it reaches the legs
options.why: Blood flows in parallel to each muscle; the legs lose flow through a reflex, not empty blood.

options.text: Fast breathing lowers blood pressure, so less blood reaches the legs
options.why: Mean arterial pressure didn't change with breathing work; leg vessels narrowed.

variants.stem: Which order matches the proposed chain from hard breathing to tired legs?

options.text: Breathing-muscle fatigue → reflex → narrower leg vessels → less leg blood flow → leg fatigue
options.why: Right: that is the metaboreflex chain.

options.text: Leg fatigue → reflex → breathing-muscle fatigue → less leg blood flow
options.why: This puts leg fatigue first; in the chain it is the end result.

options.text: Less leg blood flow → breathing-muscle fatigue → reflex → leg fatigue
options.why: Less leg blood flow is caused by the reflex, so it can't come before it.

options.text: Reflex → breathing-muscle fatigue → wider leg vessels → leg fatigue
options.why: The reflex narrows leg vessels, and it follows breathing-muscle fatigue.

variants.stem: A runner's VO₂max is 3.5 L·min⁻¹. At maximal effort breathing costs about 10% of it. How much O₂ do her breathing muscles use?

options.text: 0.35 L·min⁻¹
35 L·min⁻¹
options.why: This multiplies by 10 instead of by 0.10: 10% is a tenth.

options.text: 3.4 L·min⁻¹
options.why: This subtracts 0.10 from 3.5; take a share by multiplying.

options.text: 3.15 L·min⁻¹
options.why: That is what is left for the rest of the body (3.5 − 0.35), not what breathing uses.

variants.solution: Breathing O₂ = 0.10 × 3.5 L·min⁻¹ = 0.35 L·min⁻¹, leaving 3.15 L·min⁻¹ for everything else.

variants.stem: A cyclist near his breathing limits has a VO₂max of 5.0 L·min⁻¹; breathing costs 15% of it at maximal effort. How much O₂ do his breathing muscles use?

options.text: 0.75 L·min⁻¹
75 L·min⁻¹
options.why: This multiplies by 15 instead of by 0.15.

options.text: 4.85 L·min⁻¹
options.why: This subtracts 0.15 from 5.0; take a share by multiplying.

options.text: 4.25 L·min⁻¹
options.why: That is what is left for the rest of the body (5.0 − 0.75).

variants.stem: A triathlete's VO₂max is 4.2 L·min⁻¹; breathing costs 13% of it at maximal effort. How much O₂ do her breathing muscles use?

options.text: 0.55 L·min⁻¹
54.6 L·min⁻¹
options.why: This multiplies by 13 instead of by 0.13.

options.text: 4.07 L·min⁻¹
options.why: This subtracts 0.13 from 4.2; take a share by multiplying.

options.text: 3.65 L·min⁻¹
options.why: That is what is left for the rest of the body (4.2 − 0.55).

variants.stem: A rider pushes from heavy to maximal effort and his O₂ uptake rises by 0.5 L·min⁻¹. Why do his legs get less of that extra O₂ than at lower intensities?

options.text: Breathing takes about 39% of each extra step near the top, against 8% at moderate pace
options.why: Right: the O₂ cost of breathing rises steeply near maximal effort.

options.text: His leg muscles stop using extra O₂ once he passes 90% of VO₂max
options.why: Leg O₂ use keeps rising to VO₂max; the share going to breathing grows.

options.text: His dead space doubles as he nears maximal effort, wasting the O₂
options.why: Dead space stays about the same; it is the work of the breathing muscles that rises.

options.text: His heart stops pumping more blood once he passes heavy exercise
options.why: Cardiac output keeps rising toward maximal effort; the change is in where the O₂ goes.

variants.stem: Which session is most likely to leave a triathlete's diaphragm measurably fatigued?

options.text: A run to exhaustion at 95% of VO₂max, about 15 min
options.why: Right: diaphragm fatigue was found after exercise to exhaustion at 95% VO₂max, and it grows above 85%.

options.text: A 2 h easy ride at 60% of VO₂max
options.why: Well below 85% of VO₂max the work of breathing is too low to fatigue the diaphragm much.

options.text: Ten 10 s sprints with full recovery
options.why: Short sprints with long rests keep total breathing work low.

options.text: A 30 min steady swim at 65% of VO₂max
options.why: At this intensity breathing work stays moderate; fatigue becomes likely only above about 85%.

variants.stem: At 90% of VO₂max, a ventilator took over part of the work of breathing, and cyclists lasted 14% longer. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Less breathing work meant less reflex narrowing of leg vessels, delaying leg fatigue
options.why: Right: that is the authors' explanation, linked to the leg blood flow findings.

options.text: The ventilator gave them extra O₂ to breathe
options.why: They breathed normal air; the ventilator only reduced the muscle work of breathing.

options.text: Their arterial PO₂ rose above 150 mmHg
options.why: Arterial PO₂ can't rise above alveolar PO₂ (about 100–120 mmHg) when breathing air.

options.text: Their breathing muscles no longer needed any O₂ at all
options.why: The breathing muscles still worked, just less; the gain came from sparing blood flow, not from zero cost.

variants.stem: The unloading study tested seven trained male cyclists, who could likely tell when the ventilator was helping. What most limits applying it to all endurance athletes?

options.text: Seven trained men only, and riders knew which condition they were in
options.why: Right: a tiny, male-only sample, with no blinding, so expectation could add to the effect.

options.text: Time to exhaustion isn't a valid test of anything
options.why: It is a valid test of endurance capacity, though noisier than a time trial.

options.text: Unloading lowered O₂ uptake, which proves the study was flawed
options.why: Lower O₂ uptake is expected: the breathing muscles did less work.

options.text: Cyclists can't tell us anything about breathing at all
options.why: Breathing physiology is similar across sports; the limits are sample and blinding.

variants.stem: Does the lung limit endurance performance in healthy athletes? Which summary fits the evidence best?

options.text: Sometimes: in fit athletes near maximal effort, not at moderate intensity
options.why: Right: breathing work and EIAH can limit highly trained athletes at high intensity; at moderate intensity breathing copes.

options.text: Always: breathing is the main limit for every athlete at every pace
options.why: In most people gas exchange keeps pace and arterial O₂ holds, even at VO₂max.

options.text: Never: the lung is overbuilt, so breathing work has no effect
options.why: Loading and unloading breathing work changed leg blood flow and endurance time.

options.text: Only at altitude: at sea level the lung is never a factor
options.why: EIAH and the metaboreflex were shown at sea level.

variants.stem: Which athlete is likely to gain most from respiratory muscle training?

options.text: A recreational runner with a VO₂max of 42 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: Right: less fit people gain more, about 6% more per 10 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ lower VO₂max.

options.text: An elite runner with a VO₂max of 78 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: Highly trained athletes gain less from RMT.

options.text: A swimmer, because swimming restricts breathing
options.why: The type of sport (rowing, running, swimming, cycling) didn't change the gain; fitness did.

options.text: All equally: fitness makes no difference
options.why: The meta-regression found a clear fitness effect.

variants.stem: Which cyclist is likely to gain most from respiratory muscle training?

options.text: A club rider with a VO₂max of 45 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: Right: less fit people gain more from RMT.

options.text: A professional with a VO₂max of 80 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: Highly trained athletes gain less.

options.text: A track sprinter, because sprints need the most breath
options.why: The clear factor was fitness, not event; and the gains were shown in endurance tests.

options.text: All equally: fitness makes no difference
options.why: The meta-regression found a clear fitness effect.

variants.stem: A coach tests 6 weeks of RMT with a standard ramp test to exhaustion, before and after, and finds no change. What is the best conclusion?

options.text: Ramp tests often miss RMT gains; a time trial would show them better
options.why: Right: in the meta-analysis, constant-load, time-trial and intermittent tests detected gains, conventional incremental tests did not.

options.text: RMT has no effect on endurance performance at all
options.why: The pooled trials do show an effect; this test type is poor at detecting it.

options.text: The athlete must have trained the wrong breathing muscles
options.why: Inspiratory muscles are the target, and they do get stronger; the test is the problem.

options.text: Six weeks is always too short for any training effect
options.why: The pooled trials do show gains; the test choice explains this null result better.

variants.stem: A triathlete asks: "Will inspiratory muscle training increase my lung capacity?" What is the best answer?

options.text: Unlikely: it strengthens the inspiratory muscles, not lung function
options.why: Right: maximal inspiratory pressure rose by about 29 cmH₂O, with no effect on pulmonary function.

options.text: Yes: stronger breathing muscles mean bigger lungs
options.why: Muscle strength rose, but lung function markers didn't change.

options.text: Yes: bigger lungs are how it improves performance
options.why: Any performance gain isn't through lung size, which didn't change.

options.text: No: it has no measurable effect of any kind
options.why: It clearly strengthens the inspiratory muscles and modestly helps performance.

variants.stem: Meta-analyses find that RMT improves performance. What most limits how sure we can be?

options.text: The trials are small, and their protocols and outcomes differ
options.why: Right: small samples, differing RMT protocols and differing outcomes limit the evidence.

options.text: Meta-analyses can't be trusted at all
options.why: A meta-analysis is only as good as its trials; the method itself is sound.

options.text: No trial ever used a control or sham group
options.why: Many did: the athlete trials included sham or control groups.

options.text: RMT is too new to have been studied
options.why: Dozens of trials exist; the problem is their size and variety, not their number.
